answer: If you miss a lab, you should email the instructor as soon as possible, preferably before the session. Follow-up regarding the missed lab will be handled in person during your next lab or tutorial session.

For absences due to illness, you must provide documentation from a licensed medical professional or a walk-in clinic. You should bring this required documentation with you to your next lab or tutorial session rather than sending sensitive medical information by email.

For short-term absences of less than one week due to being unwell, the Illness Self-Declaration Form can be used instead of medical documentation to request academic consideration. After submitting the form, you should follow up with your instructor regarding flexibility for missed coursework or participation.

Supporting medical documentation must include the dates and reasons you were examined, as well as the functional impact the illness has on attending class and learning. While the Laurier Verification of Illness Form is preferred, you should check with your faculty to see if other documentation, like an original medical certificate, is accepted. It is your responsibility to ensure all requested information is included on the documentation.

answer: For labs, work must be completed individually, though groups are permitted to share only raw data.
Examples of plagiarism in labs include copying calculations, derivations, or lists from another student, or using wording that is identical or nearly identical in reports.
Plagiarism in labs results in a grade of zero on the affected lab and a referral to the course instructor and the University’s Academic Integrity process.
To avoid plagiarism in labs, students should write from their own understanding and in their own words.
The policies for the tutorial portion of the course are the same as the laboratory portion unless stated otherwise.
In tutorials, all submitted reports must be your own independent work.
In tutorials, copying, transcribing, reproducing, or copying another student's work, in whole or in part, is considered academic dishonesty.
Cheating in tutorials will be handled according to the University’s Academic Integrity Policy and may lead to disciplinary action.
Tutorial reports, which are typically written and completed in-class, must reflect a student's own independent work and reasoning.

Academic misconduct includes academic dishonesty, fraud, misconduct, and failure to respect the rights of others. A student's intention to commit misconduct is not relevant to a finding of misconduct, and hurried or careless submissions do not excuse a student from the responsibility of verifying academic integrity.
Plagiarism is defined as the unacknowledged presentation of the work of others, in whole or in part, as one's own in forms such as reports, assignments, examinations, theses, or dissertations.

Plagiarism involves passing off the thoughts, ideas, or writings of another person as your own, which includes using the words of others without proper citation or taking credit for ideas that are not your own.

Self-plagiarism is the act of submitting the same piece of work for more than one course without permission from the instructor; students are not allowed to receive course credit for the same work twice.

Cheating or copying involves the attempt to use, give, receive, or use unauthorized information during an examination (in oral or written form), or copying/allowing someone else to copy an essay, report, or examination.

answer: If you know of a conflict in advance, you must submit a request for a deferred final examination as soon as possible and at least seven calendar days before the last day of classes for the term.
If a conflict arises later, the petition must be submitted as soon as possible.

For unforeseen circumstances occurring on the day of the examination, requests should be submitted as soon as possible and no later than three business days after the scheduled date of the examination.

To receive relief for having three exams within a 24-hour period, you must submit a petition for a deferred exam through the Faculty responsible for the second course in the sequence. The deadline to submit the form is at least 7 calendar days before the final day of classes of the term.
If two or more exams are scheduled to take place simultaneously, you must complete the Final Exam Conflict Form at least 7 calendar days before the final day of classes of the term.
Requests for simultaneous exams submitted after the deadline can be submitted as a deferred exam petition to the appropriate Petitions Committee.

answer: In the laboratory, plagiarism includes using identical or nearly identical wording in reports, or copying lists, derivations, or calculations from another student.
In tutorials, copying, reproducing, or transcribing another student's work, either in whole or in part, is considered academic dishonesty.

Using resources in tutorials other than a scientific calculator, a printed course textbook, lecture notes, or homework and tutorial notes will result in a grade of zero for that week's tutorial report and may lead to more severe academic penalties.

Academic misconduct is defined in the Student Code of Conduct and Discipline as an act by a student (or students on a team project) that may result in a false evaluation or represents an attempt to unfairly gain an academic advantage, where the student knew or ought reasonably to have known it was misconduct. Intent is not relevant to a finding of academic misconduct.

Examples of academic misconduct include, but are not limited to: plagiarism, cheating, submitting the same work for multiple courses without instructor permission, impersonating someone in a test or exam, unauthorized collaboration on individual assignments, tests or exams, buying or obtaining term papers or assignments, and falsifying, misrepresenting, or forging an academic record or supporting document.

Forging doctor's notes is considered academic misconduct. Additionally, changing, omitting, or forging materials submitted to the university during the program application process can result in the revocation of an offer of admission.

answer: If you miss a lab session, you should email the instructor as soon as possible, preferably before the session, and bring required documentation to your next lab or tutorial session.

The policies for tutorials are the same as the laboratory portion, unless stated otherwise: if you miss a tutorial, email the instructor once before the session when possible and bring documentation to your next lab or tutorial.

For short-term absences of less than one week due to illness, students can use the Illness Self-Declaration Form instead of medical documentation to request academic consideration. After submitting the form, students should follow up with their instructor regarding flexibility for coursework, missed midterms, or class participation.

Supporting medical documentation should include the dates and reasons for the examination and the functional impact of the illness on learning and attendance. While the Laurier Verification of Illness Form is preferred, students should check with their faculty regarding the acceptance of alternate documentation like an original medical certificate.
If a faculty member requests a medical excuse slip, students must be examined by a WLU Health Services staff member or a qualified off-campus physician at the time of the illness.

answer: If you believe your work was graded incorrectly during the term, you should follow the instructions in the syllabus. For lab grades, you must raise questions within one week of a mark being posted, contact your section Instructional Assistant (IA) first, and if the issue is not resolved, contact the Lab Coordinator. No grade changes will be made after one week. All lab and tutorial grades are finalized before the end of the term, and requests made after final exams will not be considered.

For tutorial grades, concerns regarding marking or grade recording must be raised within one week of the work being marked. You should contact your section IA first before contacting the instructor. No grade changes will be made after this period.

The course instructor is primarily responsible for assigning the final grade. The final grade appeal process is for concerns regarding the calculation of grades and/or the application of grading criteria to submitted work. It is not for requests for relief from personal circumstances affecting academic performance, course structure, or course policy. If the syllabus does not provide a process for addressing incorrect grades, you should promptly raise the issue with the instructor. There are 4 sequential steps in the appeal process, and a student may submit only one grade appeal per course section.
Step 1 of the grade appeal process is the Instructor.

In Step 2, the chair notifies the instructor of the outcome and provides reassessed grades to the associate dean for final grade revision. The grade appeal decision (higher, lower, or unchanged) is the final grade. The chair will notify the student of the outcome via their Laurier email account, with Enrolment Services copied.

In Step 3, a student may submit a petition to the faculty offering the course no later than 10 business days after receiving the chair's decision. The petition should not include grounds or information not previously presented to the chair. If the faculty petitions committee denies the petition, a grade appeal fee will be applied to the student's account.

In Step 4, a student may appeal a decision from the Faculty Petitions Committee to the Senate Student Appeals Committee. This appeal must be submitted within 10 business days of receiving the decision from the Faculty Petitions Committee. If the Senate Student Appeals Committee rules in the student's favor, the grade appeal fee from the Petitions Committee will be refunded; if the appeal is denied, an additional grade appeal fee will be applied to the student's account.

answer: Students are not required to complete more than two final examinations in a 24 hour period.
(unverified) To receive relief from the rule regarding three exams in 24 hours, the third scheduled examination must start and finish within 24 hours of the beginning of the first examination.
To receive relief, students must complete the Final Exam Conflict Form at least seven calendar days before the final day of classes of the term.
The university reserves the right to select which examination is rescheduled.
Approved requests will have an exam scheduled to a different day and time within the examination period.

Requests submitted after the deadline can be submitted as a deferred exam petition to the appropriate Petitions Committee. If approved, the exam will be scheduled during the deferred exam period and a non-refundable deferred examination fee will be applied. The university reserves the right to select which examination is to be deferred.

For Lazaridis School of Business and Economics students, if three final exams are scheduled such that the third examination finishes within 24 hours of the beginning of the first examination, a deferral petition may be submitted at least three business days before the first of the three final examinations. In this case, the middle exam will be considered for deferral.

Students are not normally required to complete more than two final examinations in a 24-hour period. To receive relief, the third problematic exam must finish within 24 hours of the beginning of the first. The deadline to submit the form is at least 7 calendar days before the final day of classes of the term.
For these types of requests, students should submit a petition for a deferred exam through the Faculty responsible for the second course in the sequence.
Deferred exam requests of this type are exempt from the deferred examination fee and do not count toward a student’s maximum allowable deferred exams.

answer: For a first offence with no prior record, the Relevant Administrator determines the penalty after consulting with the instructor and allowing the student to present additional evidence.
Penalties for a first offence may include a grade deduction or receiving a zero for an assignment, project, test, exam, or other activity that counts toward the final course grade.
The most severe penalty that can be assigned by the Relevant Administrator is failure in the course; any other additional penalty requires a recommendation to the Dean.
Students will be notified of the penalty within ten (10) working days after the five (5) day response period ends.
A student may appeal to the Faculty Petitions Committee within ten (10) working days of receiving the Final Notice of Penalty document, and the decision of this committee is final and binding.

When determining penalties for academic misconduct, several factors may be considered, including the relative weight of the assignment, the student's academic experience, extenuating circumstances, previous offences in the Central Registry, aggravating factors, and the severity of the offence and its impact on the Laurier community. For graduate students, the work's importance to their graduate program is also considered.

answer: A Disruption is defined as occurring when academic activities are substantially interrupted or impeded due to causes such as natural disasters, health emergencies, non-Wilfrid Laurier University labour disputes, or other like causes.
Academic activity includes any work necessary for a student to meet course or program requirements or any work subject to evaluation.

To determine if an interruption is "substantial", factors such as the duration and timing of the Disruption, the impact on attendance, the availability of resources, and the impact on the timing and sequence of evaluations (like examinations, assignments, and practica) are considered.
Disruptions lasting no more than seven consecutive days are generally considered short Disruptions and will be governed by normal academic regulations where reasonably possible.

For short Disruptions, individual departments or faculties determine how much a course, lab, or seminar has been affected and what remedial action is needed. If an instructor is absent, the Department Chair, Area Head, Co-ordinator, or a designate will make changes to course procedures in consultation with the Dean.

If a course instructor believes remedial action should include rescheduling missed contact hours (such as labs or lectures) to maintain course integrity, they may take action in consultation with the Office of the Registrar and their Department Chair, Area Head, Co-ordinator, or designate.

answer: The University is committed to responding to Complaints of Gendered and Sexual Violence fairly and expeditiously, with a commitment to procedural fairness and the respectful treatment of all individuals involved.

During an investigation process, university staff or internal/external investigators will not ask students who make a Disclosure or Complaint, or seek supports and services, irrelevant questions, including those regarding the student's past sexual history or sexual expression.
Laurier offers on-campus supports and allows Survivors to choose different off-campus supports based on their needs, such as 2SLGBTQIA supports, faith or culturally based counselling, or elders.

To disclose Gendered or Sexual Violence, seek accommodations, or learn about complaint and informal intervention options, students may email svinfo.wlu.ca or phone 548-889-3517 to contact the Office of Human Rights and Conflict Management.
